slides.notes:
RECAP: Session 10 : Serverless Computing
1. Serverless Basics: No server management; event-driven execution; Function as a Service (FaaS)
2. The Execution Model: Triggers & events; the handler contract; stateless execution; concurrency
3. Cold Starts & Warm Starts: Causes of cold start; init phase vs invoke phase; mitigation strategies
4. Limits & Constraints: Execution timeout, memory, payload size & ephemeral storage
5. BaaS & Anti-Patterns: Backend as a Service: managed databases, auth & storage; when not to use serverless: long-running jobs, heavy state, steady load

Agenda for Today's Session
1. Major Cloud Providers: AWS, Azure & GCP as the primary players; IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud as additional enterprise cloud providers: market position & typical use cases
2. Service Equivalents Across Providers: Compute, storage, database & networking: same concept, different names (EC2/VM/Compute Engine; S3/Blob/Cloud Storage; RDS/Azure SQL/Cloud SQL for relational, DynamoDB/Cosmos DB/Firestore for NoSQL)
3. Machine Learning Service Comparison: Managed ML/AI offerings across AWS, Azure & GCP at a high level
4. Cloud Providers Walkthrough: The AWS console already familiar to students, shown alongside Azure Portal and GCP Console/Cloud Shell: the same task, back to back
5. Choosing a Provider: What genuinely differs (pricing, regions, service maturity, skills) vs what's cosmetic (naming, console layout)

slides.title: What is a Cloud Provider?
slides.lead: A cloud provider is a company that offers computing resources such as servers, storage, databases and networking over the internet, on a pay-as-you-go basis
slides.notes: Name all five providers together before going into any one of them. Point out that size in the diagram reflects market position, not technical capability. Interviewers often ask for all five by name, not just the top three.

slides.title: Major Cloud Providers

points.text: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure (Azure), Google Cloud (GCP): the three hyperscalers
IBM Cloud: enterprise and hybrid-cloud focused provider
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI): database and enterprise-application focused provider
Market position ranges from broad general-purpose platforms to niche enterprise specialists

slides.notes: Name all five providers together before going into any one of them. Point out that size in the diagram reflects market position, not technical capability. Interviewers often ask for all five by name, not just the top three.

slides.title: Share and Use Case
slides.lead: AWS, Azure and GCP together hold the majority of the cloud market, but each one is stronger for different kinds of workloads

cells: Largest market share, broadest service catalog
Second-largest, strong enterprise and hybrid adoption
Third-largest, strength in data and AI/ML
Data analytics, machine learning, Kubernetes-native applications

slides.notes: Point to the AWS Management Console already used in earlier demos as the home base for the largest provider. Mention that Azure Portal and GCP Console mirror the same services under different names. An interviewer may ask why a Microsoft-heavy enterprise defaults to Azure.

slides.title: Share and Use Case
slides.notes:
Point to the AWS Management Console already used in earlier demos as the home base for the largest provider. Mention that Azure Portal and GCP Console mirror the same services under different names. An interviewer may ask why a Microsoft-heavy enterprise defaults to Azure.

Visual Guidance: Horizontal bar chart beside the table showing relative market share order: AWS, then Azure, then GCP.

slides.title: Enterprise Specialists
slides.lead: Some organisations need a provider built around decades of existing enterprise systems rather than service breadth; IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) serve exactly that need

points.text: IBM Cloud: hybrid cloud and mainframe migration for regulated industries
OCI: built around Oracle database and ERP workloads
And now a major provider of large-scale AI/GPU infrastructure
Chosen for existing vendor relationships rather than broad service catalogs

note.text: Note: Five-provider comparison is covered in the post-session reading material.

slides.notes: Explain that lower market share does not mean lower capability, only a narrower target customer. A bank already running mainframes is the classic IBM Cloud example to mention aloud. Expect an interview question on why a company would ever pick a smaller provider.

slides.label: Analogy: general physician and cardiologist
slides.title: Enterprise Specialists
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A general physician treats most common ailments, but a patient with a specific heart condition goes to a cardiologist: just as IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud specialise in enterprise and database workloads rather than general-purpose breadth.

Explain that lower market share does not mean lower capability, only a narrower target customer. A bank already running mainframes is the classic IBM Cloud example to mention aloud. Expect an interview question on why a company would ever pick a smaller provider.

slides.title: Same Capability Renamed
slides.lead: Every provider sells the same four building blocks (a virtual machine, object storage, a managed database and a network boundary) under its own product name

points.text: Compute: rentable virtual machines for running applications
Storage: object storage for files accessed by key
Database: managed relational and NoSQL engines
Networking: an isolated virtual network plus traffic distribution

slides.notes: Set up the pattern before naming any product: the capability is identical, only the label changes. Ask: why would a company moving from one provider to another need a naming map rather than a new architecture?

slides.title: Translating The Label
slides.lead: When a capability already known on one provider exists on another under a different brand name, that matching is called a service equivalent: the core function is the same, though features and details can differ

points.text: Core capability and typical use case stay the same
Learning one provider’s services makes the others much faster to learn

slides.notes: Say the everyday version first (same plan, different brand) before naming it 'service equivalence'. Point out this is exactly the skill an interviewer tests when asking to map an AWS service to its Azure or GCP counterpart.

slides.label: Analogy: three telecom plans, one recharge
slides.title: Translating The Label
slides.notes:
TR analogy: Three telecom companies sell the same prepaid data-and-calls recharge under three different plan names: just as three cloud providers sell the same virtual machine capability under three different product names.

Say the everyday version first (same plan, different brand) before naming it 'service equivalence'. Point out this is exactly the skill an interviewer tests when asking to map an AWS service to its Azure or GCP counterpart.

slides.title: Virtual Machines Named
slides.lead: The raw virtual machine capability appears on each provider's console under a different product name
slides.notes: Point to the EC2 Dashboard label and note that Virtual Machines and Compute Engine are the same screen in spirit. A frequent interview question asks exactly this mapping by name.

slides.title: Object Storage Named
slides.lead: Object storage for files stored as objects, not disks, carries a different brand on each provider's console
slides.notes: Point to the S3 bucket list and note Blob Storage sits inside a Storage Account, while Cloud Storage uses buckets directly. Flag this naming difference as a common interview trap.

slides.title: Relational And NoSQL
slides.lead: Database equivalents split into two lines: managed relational (SQL) engines with fixed tables, and managed NoSQL stores for flexible, schema-less data
slides.notes: Point to the RDS row and ask which workload needs fixed schema versus flexible documents. This exact table is a standard interview ask: name the NoSQL equivalent of DynamoDB on Azure.

slides.title: Relational And NoSQL

points.text: Relational engines support fixed table schemas and joins
NoSQL stores scale horizontally without a fixed schema
Choice depends on data structure needed, not provider preference

slides.notes: Point to the RDS row and ask which workload needs fixed schema versus flexible documents. This exact table is a standard interview ask: name the NoSQL equivalent of DynamoDB on Azure.

slides.title: Network And Load Balancer Named
slides.lead: The isolated virtual network carries its own renamed line per provider; the service that spreads traffic across servers is renamed the same way

note.text: Note: Cross-cloud service equivalents are covered in the post-session reading material.

slides.notes: Mention briefly that the virtual-network naming was mapped earlier, then focus attention on the load balancer row shown here. Interviewers often ask for the AWS name of a generic 'load balancer' term.

slides.title: Beyond Pre-Built APIs
slides.lead:
Pre-trained AI APIs handle only fixed tasks
A managed Machine Learning (ML) platform gives one workspace to build, train and deploy your own model without managing servers

points.text: Built-in notebooks and GPU-backed training environments
Experiment tracking records accuracy across training runs
One-click hosting turns a trained model into an endpoint
AutoML cuts the coding needed to reach a trained model

slides.notes: Contrast calling Amazon Comprehend with building a custom fraud model from the organisation's own data. Mention AWS SageMaker Studio as the console where this workspace lives. Interview hook: ask when a pre-built API is insufficient for a use case.

slides.label: Analogy: a ready-made shirt and a tailor
slides.title: Beyond Pre-Built APIs
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A ready-made shirt off the rack is a pre-built AI API; a tailor who takes measurements and stitches to order is the managed ML platform: just as the tailor needs fabric, measurements and time, the platform needs data, training and tuning before it delivers a custom model.

Contrast calling Amazon Comprehend with building a custom fraud model from the organisation's own data. Mention AWS SageMaker Studio as the console where this workspace lives. Interview hook: ask when a pre-built API is insufficient for a use case.

slides.title: AWS Azure GCP
slides.lead: Each hyperscaler packages the full train-to-deploy workflow under one flagship platform name, reachable from its own console

cells: Unified studio: notebooks, training jobs, hosted endpoints
Visual designer, automated ML, MLOps pipelines
Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI)
Single console for AutoML and custom model training

slides.notes: Point out that SageMaker is reached from the AWS console search bar, same pattern as EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) used earlier. Say the platform name aloud, then its one capability. Exam hook: naming the three flagship ML platforms is a common interview question.

slides.title: Service Name Mapping
slides.lead: Alongside full platforms, each provider also exposes specialised pre-trained models for common tasks through a single API call
slides.notes: Remind that Rekognition and Comprehend were named earlier as AWS examples; now place the Azure and GCP equivalents beside them. Point at the task column first, then read across the row. Exam hook: matching a task to its three provider-specific service names is commonly asked.

slides.title: Service Name Mapping

points.text: Same underlying task, different service name per provider
No training data needed, model is already trained
Called over REST, response returned as structured JSON

slides.notes: Remind that Rekognition and Comprehend were named earlier as AWS examples; now place the Azure and GCP equivalents beside them. Point at the task column first, then read across the row. Exam hook: matching a task to its three provider-specific service names is commonly asked.

slides.title: Choosing The Service
slides.lead: The two layers answer different needs: a ready model for a standard task, or a workspace to build one that is genuinely custom

points.text: Pre-built API fits when the task matches an existing model
Full platform fits when training is needed on private data
AutoML sits between the two, inside the platform console

slides.notes: Close by framing the choice as standard task versus custom data, not as one provider being universally better. This same AWS console reasoning carries into the live console walkthrough coming next. Exam hook: ask when AutoML is the right middle choice.

slides.title: Console Entry Points
slides.lead: Launching a compute instance follows the same decisions on every provider; each console simply places them on a different screen, with the AWS console as the familiar reference point

points.text: AWS Console: EC2 dashboard, Launch Instance wizard
Azure Portal: Create a resource, Virtual Machine blade
GCP Console: Compute Engine, VM instances page
GCP Cloud Shell: browser-based command-line alternative

slides.notes: Open the actual AWS EC2 console live and name the launch wizard as the reference point. Mention that Azure and GCP will perform the identical task next.

slides.title: EC2 Decision Flow
slides.lead: The EC2 launch wizard, reached from the EC2 dashboard's Launch Instance button, lines up every provisioning decision in one linear screen

items.title: Name and tags
items.text: Identifies the instance for billing and search

items.title: Instance type
items.text: Sets vCPU and memory for the workload

items.title: Key pair
items.text: Sets the credential used for SSH login

items.title: Network and security group
items.text: Places the instance and opens ports

items.title: Launch
items.text: Confirms the choices and starts provisioning

slides.notes: Walk the live EC2 console top to bottom, pointing at each wizard section as it is named. Ask: which field here decides the operating system versus the one that decides sizing?

slides.title: Same Decisions Mapped
slides.lead: Azure Portal and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Console reach the identical decisions through their own blade and page layouts, confirming the task never changes
slides.notes: Demo the Azure VM creation blade and the GCP Compute Engine create-instance page back to back, pointing at the same row of the table for each. Note GCP Cloud Shell opens inside the browser with no local install, unlike a local terminal.

cells: SSH key or Cloud Shell key

slides.title: Real Vs Cosmetic
slides.lead: Picking among AWS, Azure and GCP is not a matter of which console looks friendlier; a small set of factors actually changes cost or capability, while many more only change labels on screen
slides.notes: Frame the whole section as a filter: ask of every difference, does it move cost or capability, or only the screen. Point out that this filter is what an interviewer is really testing when they ask 'why AWS over Azure'.

slides.title: Price Region Skill
slides.lead: Each factor below changes total spend, latency guarantees or hiring effort, which is why it belongs in a provider decision rather than a preference

items.title: Pricing
items.text: On-demand rates, discount tiers and data-egress fees vary by provider

items.title: Regions
items.text: Footprint differs by provider; Azure lists the most regions, while AWS builds every region with at least three availability zones

items.title: Maturity
items.text: A newer provider service may lack features an older one already shipped

items.title: Skills
items.text: Certification pools and job-market depth differ sharply across the three

props.check: Checked in practice on the AWS Pricing Calculator and the AWS Regions page

slides.notes: Explain that region count affects latency and data-residency compliance, not just marketing. Mention that service maturity means checking whether a needed feature is generally available or still in preview. Interview angle: ask why egress cost alone can flip a multi-cloud decision.

slides.title: Naming And Layout
slides.lead: The same underlying service appears under a different name and menu path on each console; this changes nothing about cost or capability

points.text: EC2, Virtual Machines, Compute Engine: one compute concept, three labels
Console menu order and dashboard layout differ with no effect on behaviour
Switching this surface costs only relearning time, not architecture or budget

slides.notes: Stress that a learner fluent in AWS is not starting over on Azure or GCP, only relearning where things sit. Tie this to the shared-responsibility and security foundations coming up, which apply the same way across all three consoles.

slides.title: Naming And Layout
slides.lead:
A provider choice is settled by pricing fit, region coverage, service maturity and team skill
Naming and layout build familiarity, but they are not criteria for choosing a provider
